$comment: Teaching content for cl_rag. Each retrieval technique is taught as the fix for a specific failure of the one before it.

knowledgePoints.name: Four problems, three benefits, four costs
knowledgePoints.teach:
Stuffing everything into the prompt fails four ways: hard length limits, degraded effectiveness on very long prompts, higher cost, slower processing.

RAG instead breaks documents into chunks and includes only the most relevant ones per question.

BenefitsCosts
focuses Claude on relevant contentrequires a preprocessing (chunking) step
scales to very large or many documentsneeds a search mechanism to find what is “relevant”
cheaper and fasterincluded chunks might miss needed context
many chunking approaches to choose between

The second problem is the subtle one: even inside the limit, a very long prompt is less effective than a short relevant one.

So RAG is not only a workaround for a size limit. Retrieving less can produce a better answer than fitting more.

questions.q: Aside from length limits and cost, what is wrong with stuffing everything into the prompt?
options: The API rejects prompts over a threshold
Effectiveness degrades on very long prompts
Long prompts simply cannot be cached at all
Claude reads only the first and last parts
questions.explain: Degradation on length is a quality argument, not just a capacity one.

questions.q: Which is a stated challenge of RAG rather than a benefit?
options: It focuses Claude on relevant content
It scales out to a great many documents
Chunks might lose the context they needed
It is both cheaper and faster to run overall
questions.explain: Cutting a document up can cut a chunk off from what made it interpretable — the problem contextual retrieval later fixes.

options: Compresses documents so that more fits in
Summarises the conversation once it grows
Chunks documents; includes only relevant ones
Moves documents to a store Claude queries
reviewQuestions.explain: Chunk and select. Compression is a different idea, and summarising history is compaction.

knowledgePoints.name: Four strategies and one default
knowledgePoints.teach:
StrategyHowTrade-off
Size-basedfixed-length character or token chunks, with overlap so sentences are not cut in halfsimplest and most reliable; works with any content including code; can still fragment meaning
Structure-basedsplit on document structure — headers, e.g. \n## cleanest chunks when formatting is guaranteed; fails on unstructured text
Sentence-basedregex into sentences, group N per chunk with overlappractical middle ground for general prose
SemanticNLP measures how related consecutive sentences are and groups by relatednessmost relevant chunks; computationally expensive and complex

Production default: size-based with overlap.

The reason is not that it produces the best chunks — semantic does. It is that it works on anything, including code and messy scraped text, and never falls over. Structure-based is the tempting one, and it is exactly as good as your assumption about the formatting is true.

questions.q: Which chunking strategy is the production default, and why?
options: Semantic — it gives the most relevant chunks
Size-based with overlap — simple and reliable
Structure-based — it gives the cleanest chunks
Sentence-based — it never cuts a sentence
questions.explain: Reliability across arbitrary input beats chunk quality on a well-behaved subset.

options: It is computationally rather expensive
It cannot make use of any chunk overlap
It makes the chunks too large to embed
It assumes formatting that may not hold
questions.explain: It is only as reliable as the formatting assumption behind it.

reviewQuestions.q: What is overlap for in size-based chunking?
options: Keeping a sentence whole across the cut
Raising recall by duplicating content
Making every chunk exactly one length
Reducing the total number of chunks made
reviewQuestions.explain: A fixed-length cut lands mid-sentence sooner or later; overlap means the sentence survives in one of the two chunks.

reviewQuestions.q: Which strategy is described as most relevant but computationally expensive?
options: Semantic
Size-based
Structure-based
Sentence-based
reviewQuestions.explain: Semantic chunking uses NLP to group by relatedness — best chunks, highest cost and complexity.

knowledgePoints.name: Meaning as a vector
knowledgePoints.teach:
A text embedding is a numerical vector representing a text's meaning. Each dimension ranges roughly −1 to +1, and individual dimensions are not human-interpretable — there is no “formality” axis to read off.

Semantic search compares those vectors, finding chunks related in meaning rather than by shared words. “How do I get my money back?” retrieves a passage about refund eligibility that shares almost no vocabulary with the question.

Anthropic does not provide embeddings. The recommended provider is VoyageAI.

That means a separate account and key — VOYAGE_API_KEY — and a model such as voyage-3-large. It is the one place in this section where the stack is not Anthropic end to end, and it is a favourite exam detail for exactly that reason.

questions.q: Where do embeddings come from in this stack?
options: VoyageAI, with its own account and key
The Anthropic embeddings endpoint itself
Computed client-side by the SDK for you
The Files API generates them on upload
questions.explain: Anthropic does not provide embeddings; VoyageAI is the recommended provider.

questions.q: What can you read off an individual embedding dimension?
options: The source document's overall topic
A sentiment score between −1 and +1
The chunk's position in the source
Nothing human-interpretable at all
questions.explain: The dimensions are not individually meaningful. Only distances between whole vectors carry information.

reviewQuestions.q: What does semantic search find that keyword search does not?
options: Exact identifiers and very rare terms
The most recently updated of documents
Chunks related in meaning, not wording
Chunks from the same document section
reviewQuestions.explain: Meaning over wording — which is also precisely why it misses exact strings.

knowledgePoints.name: The search that understood everything except the answer
knowledgePoints.teach:
Semantic search optimises for conceptual similarity. So a query for INC-2023-Q4-011 returns four incidents that are thematically similar and not the one that is literally named — because a specific identifier carries almost no meaning to embed.

BM25 (Best Match 25) is lexical, and works in four steps:

  1. Tokenise the query.
  2. Count term frequency across documents.
  3. Weight rarer terms higher — “a” gets almost nothing, INC-2023-Q4-011 gets almost everything.
  4. Return the documents with the most instances of the highest-weighted terms.

Step 3 is why it works: rarity is the signal. The rarest term in the query is usually the one that identifies the answer.

questions.q: A user searches an exact incident ID and semantic search returns four thematically similar but wrong documents. What fixes it?
options: Reranking the semantic results returned
BM25, which matches rare terms literally
Smaller chunks with a lot more overlap
A more capable embedding model instead
questions.explain: Exact-term precision is a lexical problem. No embedding model fixes it, because the identifier has no meaning to embed.

questions.q: In BM25, how are common words like “a” treated?
options: Given low weight; rarer terms score higher
Removed entirely before the scoring runs
Given high weight, being in every document
Weighted by their position in the query
questions.explain: Rarity drives weight. Common terms end up contributing almost nothing.

reviewQuestions.q: What does BM25 stand for, and what kind of search is it?
options: Best Match 25 — lexical keyword search
Binary Match 25 — a quantisation scheme
Best Match 25 — a reranking model only
Balanced Metric 25 — a hybrid scorer
reviewQuestions.explain: Best Match 25, and it is keyword search — the complement to semantic search, not a variant of it.

knowledgePoints.name: Run both, merge
knowledgePoints.teach:
Hybrid search runs semantic search and BM25 in parallel and merges the results.

You get conceptual relevance and exact-term precision at the same time, which matters because a real corpus contains both kinds of query — “how do I get a refund” and “order 88-4412-B” arrive at the same endpoint.

This is the standard production pattern for robust RAG retrieval.

Note that neither half is tuned to compensate for the other. You do not make embeddings better at identifiers; you run something else alongside them that already is.

questions.q: Your corpus gets both prose questions and part numbers. What retrieval design covers both?
options: Semantic search with a wider candidate set
BM25 with query expansion on the front
Hybrid — semantic and BM25 merged together
Semantic search over contextual chunks
questions.explain: Two retrievers, run together and merged. It is the standard production pattern.

questions.q: How do the two retrievers run in hybrid search?
options: Semantic first, then BM25 over its output
BM25 first, then semantic over its output
In parallel, with the two results merged
Whichever one returns first is the one used
questions.explain: In parallel. Chaining them would let the first stage's blind spot exclude what the second was for.

reviewQuestions.q: Why not simply improve the embedding model instead of adding BM25?
options: Better embeddings are simply unavailable
An identifier has little meaning to embed
Embeddings cannot be used with any overlap
BM25 is cheaper to run than embeddings
reviewQuestions.explain: The failure is categorical rather than a matter of quality, so it needs a different mechanism.

knowledgePoints.name: Recall first, precision second
knowledgePoints.teach:
Reranking is a second, more expensive pass that runs after initial retrieval.

  1. Pull a wide candidate set — top 20 to 50 via embeddings and BM25 — optimised for recall: get the right chunk in there somewhere.
  2. Rerank those candidates for precision using a more discriminating method — often an LLM call or a dedicated reranking model — scoring each one's actual relevance to the query.
  3. Send only the reordered top-K to Claude.

It catches the case where a fast first-pass retriever ranks a mediocre chunk above a genuinely relevant one.

The cost is latency per query, which is why it is applied to the shortlist and never to the corpus. Scoring 50 candidates carefully is affordable; scoring 500,000 is not, which is the entire reason the cheap retriever exists in front of it.

questions.q: What is the division of labour between retrieval and reranking?
options: Retrieval for precision, reranking for recall
Both aim at precision, at different scales
Retrieval for keywords, reranking semantics
Retrieval for recall, reranking for precision
questions.explain: Cast a wide net cheaply, then judge carefully within it.

questions.q: Why is reranking never applied to the whole corpus?
options: It needs embeddings the corpus may lack
It cannot score documents it has not seen
Corpus-wide, it would blow the context window
It costs real latency per candidate scored
questions.explain: It is the expensive pass by design. The cheap retriever exists precisely to make its input small.

reviewQuestions.q: How large is the candidate set typically pulled before reranking?
options: Top 3–5
Top 500
The entire corpus
reviewQuestions.explain: Wide enough that the right chunk is very likely inside, small enough to score carefully.

knowledgePoints.name: Whose revenue? Which quarter?
knowledgePoints.teach:
A chunk reading “revenue grew 3%” is nearly unretrievable and barely interpretable. Whose revenue? Which quarter? The surrounding context that answered those questions was in the paragraphs you cut away.

The fix, before embedding or indexing: run each chunk through an LLM together with the full document (or a summary of it), have it generate a short situating sentence, and prepend that to the chunk.

This chunk is from Acme Corp's Q4 2023 earnings report,
discussing automotive-division revenue.

Revenue grew 3%...

It improves semantic search (a richer embedding) and BM25 (indexable keywords the chunk lacked) at once.

And note when it happens: preprocessing time, once per chunk, not per query. That is the axis that separates it from reranking, which pays its cost on every single query.

questions.q: How does contextual retrieval differ from reranking?
options: It runs once per chunk; reranking per query
It runs at query time; reranking at index
It uses BM25; reranking uses embeddings
It replaces the chunking step entirely
questions.explain: Preprocessing-time fix versus query-time fix — pay once per chunk, or every time someone searches.

questions.q: Why does the situating sentence help BM25 as well as semantic search?
options: It shortens the chunk, raising term density
It adds indexable keywords the chunk lacked
It normalises the whole chunk's vocabulary
It does not; it only helps semantic search
questions.explain: Names that were never in the chunk become searchable terms.

reviewQuestions.q: What is passed to the LLM when generating a chunk's situating sentence?
options: The chunk on its own, and nothing else
The chunk and the user's eventual query
The chunk and its immediate neighbours
The chunk plus the document or a summary
reviewQuestions.explain: The whole document is what supplies the context the chunk lost — the query is not known yet at preprocessing time.
